k: Home About About Heritage Spices Rooted in Idukki. Built for global kitchens. Heritage Spices is an export business built around one ingredient we care deeply about: green cardamom from the hills of Idukki, Kerala. Our story Cardamom is often called the queen of spices, and Kerala’s Idukki district is one of the places it has long been grown. We started Heritage Spices to bring that harvest to buyers who care about where their ingredients begin, and who want a supplier that communicates clearly. We work directly with farmers in Idukki, and we select pods carefully for colour, aroma and condition before they are prepared for export. Our focus today is on importers, wholesalers and food and beverage businesses in the Gulf, where cardamom is part of everyday hospitality. What we stand for 01 A traceable origin We source directly from growers in Idukki, so we can talk about where your cardamom came from and who grew it. 02 Careful selection Pods are chosen for a clean aroma, even colour and good condition, because small differences are easy to taste. 03 Clear communication Written specifications, samples before orders, and straight answers on availability, packing and paperwork. Where our cardamom grows Idukki sits in the Western Ghats, a cool, humid, rainy landscape that suits cardamom. Plants grow under tall shade trees, and pods are picked by hand in rounds as they ripen. You can read more in our journal note on why Idukki cardamom has a character of its own . Who we work with We talk to spice importers and wholesalers, coffee and tea blenders, bakeries and sweet makers, and food manufacturers. If you buy for the UAE , Saudi Arabia , Qatar , Kuwait , Oman or Bahrain , we would be glad to hear from you. Buyers from other countries are welcome to get in touch too. Working

Overview Green cardamom ( Elettaria cardamomum ) is the whole dried pod of a plant grown in the shaded, rainy hills of the Western Ghats. Our pods come from Idukki, Kerala, and are sourced directly from farmers, then selected for colour, aroma and condition before export. Buying whole pods keeps the aroma protected until you are ready to use it, and it lets you inspect size, colour and cleanliness yourself, which is why many Gulf importers and coffee blenders prefer them. Common uses Arabic coffee, tea and karak, sweets and halwa, bakery and pastry, rice dishes, spice blends and beverage mixes. Read more about cardamom in Arabic coffee . Also known as Green cardamom is called elaichi in Hindi, elakkai in Tamil, elakka in Malayalam and هيل (hayl) in Arabic. It is sometimes called the “queen of spices”. How to choose and buy Pod size, colour and aroma decide quality. d: How Heritage Spices works with importers: requirements, samples, quotation, packing, documents and shipment, with FOB, CFR and CIF delivery terms explained.
k: Home Export process Export process From first message to your port. A clear, step-by-step way of working, so importers know what happens next at every stage. 01 Tell us what you need Share the size or grade, colour, aroma, quantity, packing and destination. A short message is enough to begin. 02 Approve a sample We send a sample so you can compare it with your specification. Agree what it represents before anything is committed. 03 Receive a quotation We respond with a quotation based on size, quantity, packing, destination and delivery terms. 04 Confirm the order Agree the quantity, packing, delivery terms and timing, including any seasonal peak you are planning for. 05 Packing and documents We prepare and pack your cardamom and arrange the shipping documents your destination needs, working with your clearing agent. 06 Shipment and delivery Your cardamom travels to the agreed port, usually by sea, with air freight available for small or urgent lots. Delivery terms we can discuss FOB (Free on Board) We deliver the goods to the vessel at the Indian port. You arrange and pay for freight and insurance. CFR (Cost and Freight) We pay the sea freight to your destination port. You arrange insurance and import clearance. CIF (Cost, Insurance and Freight) As CFR, with marine insurance arranged to the destination port. Documents Shipments typically involve a commercial invoice, a packing list, a bill of lading or airway bill and a certificate of origin, plus any other certificates your destination requires. Rules differ by country and can change, so we confirm the exact list with you and your clearing agent for each order. Packing Cardamom is packed in food-grade packaging. We agree the packing size with you based on your storage, turnover and market. Prices Prices depend on size

t: Cardamom in Arabic Coffee: Why the Pod Matters
d: Why green cardamom is at the heart of Gulf coffee, and what coffee blenders and importers should look for in a pod.
k: Home Journal Cardamom in Arabic coffee: why the pod matters Gulf traditions · 4 min read Cardamom in Arabic coffee: why the pod matters Why green cardamom is at the heart of Gulf coffee, and what coffee blenders and importers should look for in a pod. Across the Gulf, coffee is more than a drink. Serving Arabic coffee, often called qahwa or gahwa, is a gesture of welcome, and cardamom is what gives it much of its recognisable fragrance. Saudi, Emirati, Qatari, Kuwaiti, Omani and Bahraini versions differ in roast, colour and extra spices, but cardamom is a constant across them. Why green cardamom Arabic coffee is usually lightly roasted and brewed with ground or crushed cardamom, sometimes alongside saffron, cloves or other spices. Because the coffee is delicate, the cardamom is easy to taste. A pod that smells musty or flat will show up in the cup, while a fresh, sweet and clean pod lifts the whole drink. What blenders and importers look for People who blend or trade cardamom for coffee tend to focus on a few things. They look for a bright, even green colour, which usually points to careful picking and drying. They want a strong, sweet aroma when a pod is cracked open, and uniform size so that a blend behaves the same each time. Cleanliness matters too: whole pods with few splits, stalks or dust are easier to grind and pack. Whole pods keep their aroma Cardamom holds its fragrance best inside the pod. Once seeds are removed or ground, the aroma tends to fade faster, so many buyers prefer to buy whole green pods and process them close to the time of use. Whole pods also make it easier to check quality by eye and nose before you buy. t: Green Cardamom Sizes Explained: A Buyer’s Guide
d: A plain-language guide to how green cardamom is sized and why size, colour and uniformity all matter in a specification.
k: Home Journal Green cardamom sizes explained: what buyers should know Buyer guide · 3 min read Green cardamom sizes explained: what buyers should know A plain-language guide to how green cardamom is sized and why size, colour and uniformity all matter in a specification. When you buy green cardamom in bulk, size is one of the first things on the specification. It affects how the pods look, how they are priced and sometimes how they are used. Here is a simple way to think about it. How size is described Pod size is commonly expressed in millimetres, for example 6 mm, 7 mm or 8 mm and above, with larger pods often described as bolder. Different suppliers and markets use different grading names, so the clearest approach is to state the size you want in millimetres in your enquiry, and to approve a sample against it. Size is not the whole story A large pod is not automatically a better one. Colour, aroma, moisture and cleanliness all matter. Some buyers, such as coffee blenders, may care most about aroma and uniformity, while retail packers may care more about the look of the pod on the shelf. Uniformity helps repeat orders If you plan to buy again and again, uniformity is as important as the size itself. A lot with pods of similar size, shape and colour is easier to pack, easier to describe to your customers and easier to reorder consistently. How to specify your order In your first message, mention the size you prefer, the colour and aroma you expect, the packing you want and the country you are shipping to. t: Why Idukki Cardamom Has a Character of Its Own
d: How hills, shade, rain and careful hand harvesting shape the aroma of cardamom from the Western Ghats.
k: Home Journal Why Idukki cardamom has a character of its own Field notes · Idukki · 3 min read Why Idukki cardamom has a character of its own How hills, shade, rain and careful hand harvesting shape the aroma of cardamom from the Western Ghats. Cardamom is a plant of the forest understory. It grows best on cool, humid, shaded hillsides with steady rainfall, which describes much of the Western Ghats in Kerala. Idukki district sits in the middle of that landscape and is closely tied to the story of Indian cardamom. The surrounding region is often called the Cardamom Hills. Hills, shade and rain Elevation, regular rain and filtered light all influence how a cardamom plant grows and how its pods develop. Plantations in Idukki are commonly laid out beneath taller shade trees, which keeps the plants cool and protects the soil. Many are managed at a small scale, often by families who know their land closely. A harvest that comes in rounds Cardamom pods do not ripen all at once. A plant flowers and fruits over an extended period, so pickers return to the same plants several times in a season and choose pods at the right stage of maturity by hand. Picking at the right moment matters because it affects colour, aroma and how well a pod holds its character after drying. Why origin matters to a buyer For a buyer, origin is more than a place name. Knowing where a pod was grown, and who grew it, makes it easier to talk about consistency, to trace a lot, and to understand why one harvest smells and tastes the way it does. That is the idea behind Heritage Spices: staying close to the farmers of Idukki and keeping the conversation clear from the first sample to the final shipment. Green cardamom is judged first with the eyes and the nose. Specifications and lab tests matter too, but an experienced buyer can learn a great deal from a handful of pods on a table. Colour Good green cardamom is known for a bright, even green. Pods that look pale, patchy or bleached can point to uneven drying or long storage. Colour is not the only measure of quality, but it is often the first thing a buyer notices. Size and uniformity Pods are usually graded by size, and size is often discussed alongside price and intended use. Just as important is uniformity: a lot where the pods are similar in size, shape and colour is easier to work with and easier to repeat from one shipment to the next. See our guide to green cardamom sizes . Aroma Break a pod or crush a few seeds and smell them. The aroma should be fresh, sweet and clean. Musty, flat or dusty notes suggest moisture or old stock. Condition and cleanliness Look for whole pods with few splits, stalks or foreign matter. Moisture control matters, because pods that are too damp can deteriorate in storage and in transit. Ask for a sample The best way to judge any lot is to see it. Ask for a sample , compare it with your own specification, and talk through the points that matter for your market, such as grade, packing and how the cardamom will be used. t: Green vs Black Cardamom: Key Differences
d: Green and black cardamom are different spices with different flavours and uses. Here is how to tell them apart before you order.
k: Home Journal Green vs black cardamom: the differences buyers should know Buyer guide · 4 min read Green vs black cardamom: the differences buyers should know Green and black cardamom are different spices with different flavours and uses. Here is how to tell them apart before you order. Many first-time buyers ask whether green and black cardamom are the same spice at different stages. They are not. They come from different plants and are used in different ways, so ordering the wrong one is a costly mistake. Appearance Green cardamom pods are small, light green and oval with thin papery skin, and are usually sold whole. Black cardamom pods are much larger, dark brown to black, wrinkled and rough. Flavour and aroma Green cardamom has a sweet, floral, citrus-like fragrance. Black cardamom is smoky, camphor-like and earthy, because the pods are traditionally dried over fire. The two are not interchangeable in a recipe. Where each is used Green cardamom is the spice in chai, Arabic coffee, desserts, sweets and rice dishes such as biryani and pulao. Black cardamom is used mainly in savoury, slow-cooked dishes and some spice blends. Where they come from Green cardamom (Elettaria cardamomum) is grown in warm, humid, shaded hills, and Idukki in Kerala is one of India’s best-known growing areas. Black cardamom (Amomum subulatum) is typically grown in cooler Himalayan regions. What this means when ordering Always state the spice, form (whole pods) and size or grade in your enquiry. If you are buying for Arabic coffee, chai or sweets, you need green cardamom. Heritage Spices supplies whole green cardamom from Idukki. t: Indian Cardamom Grades: AGEB, AGB, AGS
d: Quick answer: Indian green cardamom is graded by pod size and colour, from extra bold (largest) to bold and superior. Millimetre ranges vary by trader.
k: Home Journal Indian cardamom grades explained: AGEB, AGB and AGS Buyer guide · 4 min read Indian cardamom grades explained: AGEB, AGB and AGS Quick answer: Indian green cardamom is graded by pod size and colour, from extra bold (largest) to bold and superior. Millimetre ranges vary by trader. If you buy Indian green cardamom you will meet grade names such as AGEB, AGB and AGS. They look confusing at first, but the idea is simple: larger, greener, more uniform pods are placed in higher grades. What the letters stand for AG usually stands for Alleppey Green, a trade name that goes back to the port through which Kerala cardamom was traditionally sold. EB means extra bold, B means bold and S means superior. So AGEB is Alleppey Green Extra Bold, AGB is Alleppey Green Bold and AGS is Alleppey Green Superior. How the grades differ In general, AGEB is the largest and most striking grade, AGB is a slightly smaller bold pod, and AGS and smaller grades follow. Each trader and market sets its own millimetre ranges, so never assume that one supplier’s AGB matches another’s. Ask for the size range in millimetres and a physical sample. Bigger is not always better Larger pods look impressive and are often chosen for retail packs and gifting. Coffee, chai and masala blenders may prefer a smaller grade with excellent aroma and good uniformity, which can suit their use just as well. Choose the grade for your use, not for the name. What else to check besides grade Grade only describes size and general appearance. Also check colour, aroma, moisture, the share of broken or empty pods and cleanliness. t: How to Store Green Cardamom to Keep Its Aroma
d: Quick answer: keep whole green cardamom pods in an airtight container, away from heat, light and moisture, and grind only what you need.
k: Home Journal How to store green cardamom so it keeps its aroma Storage guide · 3 min read How to store green cardamom so it keeps its aroma Quick answer: keep whole green cardamom pods in an airtight container, away from heat, light and moisture, and grind only what you need. Cardamom is valued for its aroma, and aroma is exactly what is lost when it is stored badly. The good news is that the rules are simple, for a home kitchen and for a warehouse. Keep it whole The pod protects the seeds. Whole green pods hold their fragrance far longer than loose seeds or ground powder, so store and buy whole pods and crush them just before use. Airtight, cool and dark Use an airtight container such as a glass jar or a sealed food-grade bag, and keep it somewhere cool, dry and out of sunlight. Heat and light speed up the loss of aroma, and moisture can lead to mould. Keep it away from strong smells Spices absorb nearby odours. Do not store cardamom beside strong-smelling goods such as dried fish, chemicals or pungent spices. For wholesalers and warehouses Store bags off the floor, away from walls, in a dry and ventilated room. Check moisture before accepting stock, rotate older lots first and keep a sealed sample from each delivery for comparison. Our buying checklist explains what to look for when you receive a lot. Buying cardamom that stores well Properly dried, clean pods keep better. Heritage Spices supplies whole green cardamom from Idukki and shares packing details on enquiry. k: Home Journal Cardamom export documents from India: a buyer’s checklist Importer checklist · 4 min read Cardamom export documents from India: a buyer’s checklist Quick answer: a cardamom shipment from India typically needs an invoice, packing list, bill of lading, certificate of origin and phytosanitary certificate. Importers in the Gulf often ask which documents come with a cardamom shipment from India. The exact list depends on your country, your product and your clearing agent, so treat this as a starting checklist and confirm requirements locally. Commercial documents A commercial invoice states what is sold, the quantity, the value and the terms, such as FOB, CFR or CIF. A packing list describes how the goods are packed. For sea freight there is a bill of lading, and for air freight an airway bill. Origin and plant health A certificate of origin states that the goods come from India. A phytosanitary certificate, issued by the relevant Indian authority, confirms the plant product has been inspected for pests. Many countries ask for one for spices, so check your rules. Exporter registrations In India, exporters generally need an Importer-Exporter Code (IEC), and spice exporters are usually registered with the Spices Board. t: Cardamom Packing for Export: What to Specify
d: Quick answer: specify the bag or carton type, net weight per pack, labelling and how pallets are loaded, so the cardamom arrives dry, clean and intact.
k: Home Journal Cardamom packing for export: what importers should specify Importer checklist · 3 min read Cardamom packing for export: what importers should specify Quick answer: specify the bag or carton type, net weight per pack, labelling and how pallets are loaded, so the cardamom arrives dry, clean and intact. Good cardamom can be damaged by poor packing. Moisture, crushing and strong odours all reduce quality on the way to the port and across the sea. Agree packing details with your supplier before the order is confirmed. Protect against moisture and smell Cardamom absorbs moisture and nearby odours. Ask that it is packed in clean, food-grade material in a dry condition, and loaded away from strong-smelling cargo. Decide the pack size Importers usually choose a pack size that suits their warehouse and customers, from larger bags for repacking to smaller packs for direct sale. Tell the supplier the net weight per bag or carton you want. Labelling Say what must appear on each pack, such as product name, origin, net weight and batch or lot number, and any labelling your country requires. Your clearing agent can confirm the local rules. Loading and shipping Ask how packs are stacked and loaded, and whether pallets or cartons will be used. For small or urgent lots, air freight is an option, while large lots usually go by sea. Delivery terms such as FOB, CFR or CIF decide who arranges and pays for each step, and our export process page explains them. Confirm before you pay Put the packing type, net weight, labelling and loading plan in writing with the quotation, along with the grade and size.
